{{Use American English|date = March 2019}}
{{Short description|Summation formula}}
{{distinguish|Christoffel–Darboux formula}}
In [[mathematical analysis]], '''Darboux's formula''' is a formula introduced by  {{harvs|txt|authorlink=Jean Gaston Darboux|first=Gaston|last=Darboux|year=1876}} for [[Summation|summing]] [[infinite series]] by using [[integral]]s or evaluating integrals using infinite series. It is a generalization to the [[complex plane]] of the [[Euler–Maclaurin formula|Euler–Maclaurin summation formula]], which is used for similar purposes and derived in a similar manner (by repeated [[integration by parts]] of a particular choice of [[integrand]]). Darboux's formula can also be used to derive the [[Taylor series]] from [[calculus]]{{cn|date=March 2022}}{{dubious|reason=This could only be true if a proof of Darboux's formula that DOES NOT RELY on the Taylor series, since otherwise such a proof deriving the Taylor series would be circular. Is it actually the case that Darboux's formula does not use the Taylor series?|date=March 2022}}.

==Statement==
If ''φ''(''t'') is a polynomial of degree ''n'' and ''f'' an analytic function then

: <math> 
\begin{align}
      & \sum_{m=0}^n (-1)^m (z - a)^m \left[\varphi^{(n - m)}(1)f^{(m)}(z) - \varphi^{(n - m)}(0)f^{(m)}(a)\right] \\
  = {} & (-1)^n(z - a)^{n + 1}\int_0^1\varphi(t)f^{(n+1)}\left[a + t(z - a)\right]\, dt.
\end{align}
</math>

The formula can be proved by repeated [[integration by parts]].

==Special cases==

Taking ''&phi;'' to be a [[Bernoulli polynomial]] in Darboux's formula gives the [[Euler–Maclaurin summation formula]]. Taking ''φ'' to be (''t''&nbsp;−&nbsp;1)<sup>''n''</sup> gives the formula for a [[Taylor series]].
